absent: Locking and concurrency rules for FFA device, driver, message, memory and notifier operations.
State machines for RXTX mapping, message transactions, memory share and lend lifecycle, and notification bind and send.
SMCCC conduit getter implementation and HVC and SMC register-level mechanics and result layout.
Enabled-configuration behavior behind the fallback stubs for FFA, MPAM, ACPI and SDEI.
MPAM controller and resource-instance structures and ACPI table layout.
SDEI enable, dispatch, priority and masking semantics beyond the fallback.
ASN.1 encoding and decoding logic beyond class and method constants.
Memory-operation buffer ownership, scatterlist handling and error propagation.

findings.text: SMCCC 1.2 invocation obtains a conduit through the 1.1 getter, dispatches caller supplied argument and result register blocks to the HVC or SMC helper matching that conduit, and otherwise records a not-supported result when a result block is present and reports no conduit. The observed conduit value is returned to the caller.

FFA function identifiers are standard-owner fast calls parameterized by 32- or 64-bit calling convention and a function number. Numbers 0x60 through 0x69 denote error, success, interrupt, version, features, RX release, RXTX map, RXTX unmap, partition-info get and ID get, with 64-bit twins for success and RXTX map at the same numbers.

Messaging uses 32-bit numbers 0x6A through 0x70 for poll, wait, yield, run, send, direct request and direct response, with 64-bit twins for direct request and response, plus 0x86 for send2 and 64-bit-only 0x8D and 0x8E for direct request2 and response2.

Memory management uses 32-bit numbers 0x71 through 0x7B for donate, lend, share, retrieve request and response, relinquish, reclaim, operation pause and resume, and fragment RX and TX, with 64-bit twins for donate, lend, share and retrieve request, plus 0x88 and 0x89 for permission get and set with 64-bit twins.

Notifications and miscellaneous controls use 32-bit numbers 0x7C through 0x85 for normal-world resume, notification bitmap create and destroy, bind, unbind, set, get, info get, RX acquire and SPM ID get, with a 64-bit twin for info get, plus 0x87 for secondary endpoint register with 64-bit twin, 0x8A console log, 64-bit-only 0x8B partition-info-get-regs, and 0x8C EL3 interrupt handle.
The native FFA identifier selector resolves to the 64-bit twin in one build alternative and to the 32-bit name in the other, so callers write one logical name and obtain the width matching the build.

FFA result codes are small signed integers with zero meaning success and minus one through minus nine meaning not supported, invalid parameters, no memory, busy, interrupted, denied, retry, aborted and no data in that order.
FFA version words carry the major number in bits 30 to 16 and the minor number in bits 15 to 0, with helpers to extract each half and to pack a pair, and with defined versions 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2.
The FFA page size is 4 KiB. RXTX minimum-size feature values use 0 for 4 KiB, 1 for 64 KiB and 2 for 16 KiB under a two-bit mask. The version 1.0 partition-info record size is eight bytes.

An FFA device carries a numeric identifier, capability properties, a VM identifier, a flag selecting 32-bit messaging mode, a UUID, an embedded generic device, and a pointer to the FFA operations table. A companion identifier holds only a UUID, and an FFA driver holds a name, probe and remove callbacks, an identifier table and an embedded generic driver, with helpers to recover each container from the embedded member.
FFA driver-private data lives in the embedded generic device driver-data slot; the FFA set and get helpers forward to the generic device set and get operations.

In the routed fallback configuration device registration yields a null handle, both device unregister helpers do nothing, driver registration reports invalid argument, and validity checking reports false.

Driver registration macros supply the current module owner and name automatically, and a module-level macro ties a driver instance to those register and unregister helpers for module lifetime management.

Partition information holds a 16-bit identifier, a 16-bit execution-context count, a 32-bit property word and a UUID. Property bits report direct-request receive, direct-request send, indirect messaging, notification receive, AArch64 execution, and request2 receive and send.

A property test reports whether a device property word contains a requested bit. Convenience predicates cover notification receive, indirect messaging and direct receive, while direct request2 receive additionally requires that 32-bit mode be off.

Direct message payloads are either five register-width words or an array of fourteen register-width words. An indirect message header carries flags, an offset, a combined sender-receiver identifier, a size, reserved words and a UUID.

Memory sharing descriptors chain a top region header to per-receiver access entries and then to a composite range holding constituent base addresses and 4 KiB page counts with total and count fields. The top header carries sender, attributes, flags, a 64-bit global handle, tag and endpoint-list sizing and offset; each access entry carries receiver, permission byte, flag byte, composite offset, implementation-defined bytes and reserved space.

Memory attribute encodings distinguish executable, non-executable, writable and read-only permissions, normal versus device types, write-back versus non-cacheable caching, device GRE variants, non and outer and inner shareability, clear-on-transfer, time-slice permission, share and lend and donate retrieve types with in-response marker, an alignment hint with shift, a constituent index offset, a self-borrower flag, and low and high 32-bit halves of the 64-bit handle with pack and extract helpers.

Descriptor layout depends on negotiated version: endpoint offset and later reserved words exist only after 1.0, and implementation-defined bytes in each access entry exist only from 1.2. Size helpers return the truncated or full top-header size and access-entry size accordingly, and a descriptor-offset helper adds the endpoint array extent to the version-appropriate base.

FFA functionality is grouped into info, messaging, memory, CPU and notifier operation tables aggregated by one top table. Info covers version and partition lookup; messaging covers 32-bit mode selection, synchronous send-receive in both widths and indirect send; memory covers reclaim, share and lend with scatterlist and attribute arguments; CPU covers run of a virtual CPU; notifier covers schedule-receive and partition and framework notification registration, relinquish and send with callbacks carrying CPU, notification identity, user data and optional buffer.

MPAM interface kind distinguishes real MMIO management controllers from PCC-backed ones, resource class distinguishes cache, main memory and unknown classes, and a default class identifier value of 255 is defined.

In the routed fallback configuration ACPI resource parsing, MSC counting and resource-instance creation report invalid argument, resctrl monitor and allocation enable and disable do nothing, and monitor-value rounding returns its input unchanged.

The routed SDEI fallback reports a zero entry point regardless of conduit, defines an event callback receiving event number, interrupted register state and private argument and returning an integer, and makes local mask and unmask report success while ACPI init and handler abort do nothing.
A registered SDEI event holds interrupted register state for architecture use plus callback, callback argument, event number and priority.
Array helpers compute element count from total and element sizes with an array-type check and derive an end pointer one past the last element.
ASN.1 tag classes are universal, application, context and private with values zero through three under a two-bit class mask, and methods are primitive zero and constructed one with a constructed bit.

Callers must handle fallback failures and width gating: device registration can yield null, driver registration can fail, validity can be false, direct request2 receive is unavailable in 32-bit mode, and handle values must be split and reassembled through low and high halves rather than truncated.
Asynchronous and driver entries are the FFA probe and remove callbacks, the SDEI event callback, and the schedule-receive and notification callbacks registered through the notifier operations.
